title: Friendship and the Staircase
text:
After the Second World War, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology housed married veteran students and their families in two complexes called Westgate and Westgate West. Couples were assigned apartments more or less as they came free, so they had no say in who their neighbors would be. For the social psychologists Leon Festinger, Stanley Schachter and Kurt Back, this was a natural experiment.

They asked residents which three people in the housing project they saw most often socially. The answers followed the floor plan with striking regularity. People named their next-door neighbors far more often than those two doors away, and those two doors away more than people at the end of the hall. Friendships across floors were rarer still.

Small details of architecture mattered. Residents whose apartments sat near the foot of a staircase or beside the mailboxes, where others passed every day, were chosen as friends more often than people in quieter spots on the same floor. Friendship, the researchers concluded, grows from the countless small encounters that physical layout makes likely, not only from shared interests or personality.
lesson: Friendships grow from repeated casual contact. If you want closer ties with someone, put yourself on their daily path and give small encounters a chance to add up.
people: Leon Festinger, Stanley Schachter, Kurt Back
location: Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, USA
source: Festinger, L., Schachter, S., and Back, K. (1950). Social Pressures in Informal Groups: A Study of Human Factors in Housing. Harper.
